title: How North Korea Pulled Off the Biggest Heist in History

summary.headline: North Korea steals $6.3 billion from Binance in historic crypto heist
summary.tldr: North Korean state hackers executed the largest theft in history, taking roughly $6.3 billion from crypto exchange Binance by exploiting human security weaknesses and smart contract rules. Stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle stepped in to freeze $2.4 billion of the stolen funds, while Binance promised to cover all customer losses despite facing $4.7 billion in withdrawals.

key_points.point: North Korea's cyber unit, Trader Trader, stole roughly $6.3 billion from Binance, taking most of it within the first 30 minutes of the attack.
key_points.why_it_matters: This represents the largest single heist in history, surpassing both conventional bank robberies and previous cryptocurrency breaches.

key_points.point: Hackers breached Binance's signing system via a months-long social engineering effort involving fake job interviews, malware, and Ethereum feature EIP-7702 to conduct blind signing.
key_points.why_it_matters: The breach succeeded not by breaking underlying blockchain cryptography, but by exploiting human error and automated signing permissions within corporate software.

key_points.point: Centralized stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle froze approximately $2.4 billion of the stolen tokens shortly after the attack.
key_points.why_it_matters: This highlights how major crypto networks rely on centralized intermediaries capable of acting like traditional banks to halt or reverse transactions during crises.

key_points.point: Binance froze withdrawals until Sunday morning, during which customers pulled out $4.7 billion (about 3% of assets), and pledged to cover all remaining losses.
key_points.why_it_matters: While exchange liability terms limited legal obligation to pay, large trading revenue allowed Binance to absorb losses to protect corporate reputation and customer retention.

key_points.point: Binance kept its emergency reserve fund in Bitcoin, which dropped by about $100 million right when the market reacted to the hack.
key_points.why_it_matters: Matching asset reserves directly to liabilities can fail if market panic lowers the market value of the collateral asset during a crisis.

summary.lesson: Holding emergency reserve funds in volatile assets creates wrong-way risk, where the value of collateral declines simultaneously with an increase in liability obligations.
opinions_and_predictions: Elliptic told the FT that the hack was almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in human history.
Alexander Shirtcliff (lawyer at Edwin Coe) noted that Binance's terms of service limit customer liability, meaning its pledge to cover losses is not legally binding.
Matt Levine stated that stablecoin issuers using blacklist functions results in centralized intermediaries performing a quasi-law enforcement function.
Tom Robinson (Elliptic) expects stolen funds to eventually be sold off to over-the-counter brokers who ask few questions.
Kelly Yee (Talos) noted that the market treated the hack as an operational shock rather than a systemic failure.

glossary.definition: An internet-connected crypto wallet that automatically processes instant user deposits and withdrawals without manual approval.
glossary.example: Binance held $2.5 billion in an online hot wallet to payout automatic Ethereum requests.

glossary.definition: The act of authorizing a digital transaction or smart contract without reading or verifying the underlying code.
glossary.example: Binance's automated system engaged in blind signing when approving the hacker's payload.

glossary.definition: A cryptocurrency designed to maintain a stable value by pegging to a fiat currency like the US dollar.
glossary.example: Tether and Circle issued stablecoins that were frozen following the attack.

glossary.definition: A legal scenario where a customer seeks out a foreign financial firm entirely on their own initiative without active marketing by the firm.
glossary.example: Binance cited reverse solicitation to explain why European residents continued to use its exchange.

glossary.definition: A risk management tactic where an entity matches assets and liabilities in the same currency or asset type.
glossary.example: Binance used Bitcoin to back customer Bitcoin obligations as a natural hedge.

summary.quality_note: Host Patrick Boyle provides detailed factual reporting sourced from major news outlets (FT, Bloomberg, WSJ) along with financial analysis and commentary.
